newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finnish PM sees stability pact if Germany gives in.
newsitem.headline: Finnish PM sees stability pact if Germany gives in.

text.p: Finnish Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen said on Wednesday that European Union leaders could agree on a stability pact if Germany gave in and agreed to more flexible terms than it has proposed.
"More flexibility is needed than Germany has proposed," Lipponen told a news conference.
"Whether the budget stability pact will be reached is up to whether Germany will give in," he said.

He said it would be "difficult, even fruitless to define too exactly" the economic circumstances which would allow a government inside the planned third stage of Europe's Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) to avoid sanctions if its budget deficit exceeded three percent of GDP.

Germany wants an economic downturn defined numerically while others, in particular France, say it would be preferable to have a more flexible approach that takes account of the economic differences between EU countries.
The stability pact is among top issues on the agenda of the weekend EU summit in Dublin.
The EU's monetary committee was meeting on Wednesday in a last-ditch effort to resolve differences over the pact.

But EU monetary sources said they did not expect the meeting of national treasury and central bank officials to settle the dispute and predicted the group would simply lay out options for a budget disciplinary accord for EU finance ministers who meet in Dublin on Thursday.
European Commission President Jacques Santer said on Wednesday in Brussels that the EU was close to reaching agreement on the budget stability pact.

Bank of France Governor Jean-Claude Trichet, speaking to Germany's Die Zeit weekly in a report published on Wednesday, said he had "no doubt" European countries would iron out their differences and agree on the pact.
